cues.en: Welcome. I'm really honored to have, to be able to introduce our speaker today. Jeff Hinton is from the University of Toronto. He graduated from Cambridge in 1970 with a Bachelor of Arts in Experimental Psychology and from Edinburgh in 1978 with a PhD in Artificial Intelligence.
cues.zh: 欢迎。很荣幸能介绍今天的演讲者。Jeff Hinton 来自多伦多大学。他1970年毕业于剑桥大学，获实验心理学学士；1978年毕业于爱丁堡大学，获人工智能博士学位。

cues.en: We barbarians south of the Canadian border don't take much stock in pedigree, but as a computer scientist, I was, I couldn't help but notice that Jeff is the great, great grandson of the logician George Boole. Very cool. Among his many achievements, Jeff co-invented Boltzmann machines along with Terry Sosnowski and introduced back propagation for training multilayer neural networks with Paul Wehrbusch.
cues.zh: 我们这些加拿大边境以南的“野蛮人”不太看重血统，但作为计算机科学家，我忍不住注意到 Jeff 是逻辑学家 George Boole 的曾曾孙。太酷了。在他众多成就中，Jeff 与 Terry Sosnowski 共同发明了玻尔兹曼机，并与 Paul Wehrbusch 引入了用于训练多层神经网络的反向传播。

cues.en: David Rummelhart and Ron Williams. He's the founding director of the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit at University College London, which is one of the premier places to study computational neuroscience in the world. His students comprise a stellar list of computer scientists in machine learning and computer vision. They include Rick Selesky, Richard Zemel, Radford Neal, Karl Rasmussen, Brendan Frey, and EYT Tay.
cues.zh: David Rummelhart 和 Ron Williams。他是伦敦大学学院 Gatsby 计算神经科学中心的创始主任，该中心是全球研究计算神经科学最顶尖的地方之一。他的学生包括机器学习与计算机视觉领域一批杰出的计算机科学家：Rick Selesky、Richard Zemel、Radford Neal、Karl Rasmussen、Brendan Frey 和 EYT Tay。

cues.en: all research scientists, well known by many of us. He was elected to the, to the Royal Society in 1998, received the Ichkai Research Excellence Lifetime Achievement Award in 2005. And despite these numerous awards and popularity as an invited speaker and thesis advisor, he continues to be amazingly productive and inventive.
cues.zh: 他们都是研究科学家，很多人耳熟能详。他1998年当选英国皇家学会院士，2005年获 Ichkai 研究卓越终身成就奖。尽管获奖无数，作为受邀演讲者和论文导师也很受欢迎，他依然保持着惊人的高产和创造力。

cues.en: If you haven't heard about Deep Belief Networks, Contrastive Diversions, Products of Experts, The Wake Sleep Algorithm, Symantecaching, or any of a host of other inventions of Jeff, you probably don't know what ICML or NIP stands for either. Back in January, Jan LeCun, one of the many computer scientists that Jeff has influenced, started a machine learning related meme by writing Jeff Hinton facts.
cues.zh: 如果你没听说过深度信念网络、Contrastive Diversions、专家乘积、Wake-Sleep 算法、Symantecaching，或 Jeff 的其他一大堆发明，那你大概也不知道 ICML 或 NIP 代表什么。今年一月，Jeff 影响过的众多计算机科学家之一 Jan LeCun 通过写“Jeff Hinton facts”发起了一个机器学习相关的梗。

cues.en: This is an analog of Jeff Norris facts, which I didn't know about before I found this out. So here's a couple of them. Jeff Hinton doesn't need to make hidden units. They hide by themselves when he approaches. Jeff Hinton once built a neural network that beat Chuck Norris on MNIST. After an encounter with Jeff Hinton, support vectors become unhinged.
cues.zh: 这类似“Jeff Norris facts”，我之前发现这事前并不知道。这里有几个例子。Jeff Hinton 不需要构造隐藏单元，他一靠近，它们就自己藏起来。Jeff Hinton 曾构建一个在 MNIST 上击败 Chuck Norris 的神经网络。遭遇 Jeff Hinton 后，支持向量会变得失控。

cues.en: And for today's introduction, I created a mashup from two of Jan's facts. It goes, never interrupt one of Jeff Hinton's talks. He will make you regret without bounds. Now that's really unfair because Jeff's one of the sweetest guys I know. He doesn't have a mean field in his body. And you'll have ample opportunity to test this because he's going to be around with us for most of the summer. So without further ado, Jeff.
cues.zh: 为了今天的介绍，我把 Jan 的两个段子混编了一下。内容是：永远别打断 Jeff Hinton 的演讲，他会让你后悔到无界。这其实很不公平，因为 Jeff 是我认识的最友善的人之一。他身体里没有一丝“平均场”。你们会有充足机会验证这一点，因为他整个夏天大部分时间都会和我们在一起。废话少说，Jeff。

cues.en: So today I'm going to talk about a new idea in machine learning. And it also has implications for a couple of major problems in biology. So the main theme of the talk is going to be this new idea in machine learning. But it was partly inspired by some work on the theory of evolution.
cues.zh: 今天我要讲机器学习中的一个新想法。它还对生物学中的几个重大问题有启示。所以这场演讲的主线将是机器学习中的这个新想法。但它部分受到一些进化论工作的启发。

cues.en: worked on it a long time ago and gave up on it because I didn't do the experiments properly. And then Papa Dimitri came to Toronto and gave a talk. And I thought, that's the same idea. And so I went back and did the experiments properly, and it really works nicely. So to explain something in the theory of evolution, it also explains something about how neurons communicate. So in the theory of evolution, there's a problem with sexual reproduction. And the problem is that to be nice and fit, you need your genes to be working well together.
cues.zh: 很久以前研究过它，后来放弃了，因为我没有把实验做对。然后 Papa Dimitri 来到多伦多，做了一场报告。我心想，这是同一个想法。于是我回去把实验认真做了一遍，效果确实很好。所以，要解释进化论中的某件事，它也能解释神经元如何通信。在进化论中，有性生殖存在一个问题。问题在于，要表现良好、适应性强，你的基因需要很好地协同工作。

cues.en: So you find a nice set of genes that are well co-adapted. And then you mate, and half the genes disappear. This is a simple model of what goes on. Half the genes disappear. And so now you don't have your big set of co-adapted genes anymore, so you don't work so well. And that is a real puzzle. Why isn't that a bad thing?
cues.zh: 于是你找到一组很好的、协同适应的基因。然后你交配，一半的基因消失了。这是所发生情况的一个简单模型。一半的基因消失。现在你不再拥有那一大组协同适应的基因，所以你表现就不那么好。这确实是个谜。为什么这不算坏事？

cues.en: The paper by Livnath Papabdumitra and Feldman in 2008 claims that the whole point of sexual reproduction is to break up these co-adaptations. And there's two reasons why that might be a good idea. One is for long-term optimization. So in the short term, maybe it's bad. But it gets you out of situations in which you have to change lots of things all at the same time to make any progress. So it might have long-term optimization. You don't have much evidence of that from
cues.zh: Livnath Papabdumitra 和 Feldman 在 2008 年的论文声称，有性生殖的全部意义就在于打破这些协同适应。这可能是个好主意，原因有两个。一个是为了长期优化。所以在短期，也许它是坏事。但它能让你摆脱那种必须同时改变许多东西才能取得任何进展的处境。所以它可能带来长期优化。你还没有太多这方面的证据，来自

cues.en: the machine learning perspective you had. The other thing is it might make you more robust against changes in the environment. So if the environment changes, then if you have a big complex co-adaptation that produces an effect that you want by depending on lots of different genes, it's liable something will get messed up.
cues.zh: 你已有的机器学习视角。另一件事是，它可能让你对环境变化更鲁棒。所以如果环境改变，而你有一个大型复杂的协同适应，它依赖许多不同基因来产生你想要的效果，那么很可能某处会出问题。

cues.en: But if instead of that, you have lots of smaller co-adaptations that achieve the function in many different ways using a few genes working together, then when you mess with the environment, some of those ways are more likely to survive. And it turns out that's a big effect. The other biological issue is how neurons communicate. So cortical neurons do a lot of signal processing, and they're very good at it. And yet, they don't send real numbers to each other.
cues.zh: 但如果不是这样，而是有许多更小的协同适应，它们用少数基因协同工作，以许多不同方式实现该功能，那么当你扰乱环境时，其中一些方式更可能存活下来。事实证明，这是一个很大的效应。另一个生物学问题是神经元如何通信。皮层神经元做大量信号处理，而且非常擅长。然而，它们彼此之间并不发送实数。

cues.en: As far as we can tell, they send these spikes of activity that are one or zero. And the timing of the spikes is random. Now, this is completely crazy, because for the same amount of energy, they could send a spike with precise timing relative to some oscillation, say. And so they could communicate an analog value by the time of the spike. And the question is, why don't they do that? OK. And I'm going to try and answer both those questions when I've told you about this idea of machine learning.
cues.zh: 据我们所知，它们发送的是取值为 1 或 0 的活动脉冲。而且脉冲的时间是随机的。现在，这完全疯狂，因为以同样的能量，它们本可以发送相对于某种振荡、比如具有精确定时的脉冲。这样它们就能通过脉冲的时间来传递一个模拟值。问题是，它们为什么不这样做？好。等我讲完这个机器学习中的想法后，我会尝试回答这两个问题。

cues.en: One reason why we sort of need to understand why neurons can communicate with single spikes like this is because we would like to make really big neural nets that are implemented on many cores. And so the states of neurons, some neurons are going to be in one core and some neurons in another core. You need to communicate the states of neurons between cores. And so you'd like that to be low bandwidth. And if they only really need one bit to communicate their state, that's a win by a factor of 32 over what people are doing at present.
cues.zh: 我们需要理解神经元为什么能用单个脉冲这样通信，一个原因是我们想造很大的神经网络，运行在很多核上。神经元状态有的在一个核里，有的在另一个核里。你需要跨核传递神经元状态。所以你希望带宽低。如果它们真的只需一个比特来传递状态，那相比目前做法就是 32 倍的优势。

cues.en: So on the face of it, it seems very hard to believe that one bit could be a better thing to send than analog value. I think that's because as engineers, we're used to sort of doing signal processing. You do things like you fit some data by assuming there's a linear dynamical system, and you fit a linear dynamical model. And to do that, you want to use real numbers. That's not the kind of problem the brain's solving.
cues.zh: 表面上看，很难相信发送一个比特会比发送模拟值更好。我想这是因为作为工程师，我们习惯做信号处理。比如假设存在线性动态系统，然后拟合一个线性动态模型。要这么做，你就得用实数。但大脑要解决的不是这类问题。

cues.en: The engineer sells them from where they come to the problem with a good idea of what model they want to fit, and now they want to identify the parameters. The brain comes to this completely incomprehensible world with huge amounts of input data. It's a real confusing mess. And the right thing to do in that situation is to fit a gazillion different models. You don't want to fit one specific model really nicely. You want to fit a gazillion different models and then use the wisdom of crowds.
cues.zh: 工程师带着清晰的模型设想来到问题前，现在要辨识参数。大脑面对的是完全不可理解的世界，输入数据巨大，一团混乱。这种情况下正确的做法是拟合无数个不同模型。不是精细地拟合某一个特定模型，而是拟合无数模型，然后利用群体智慧。

cues.en: That is, when someone asks you a question, you get all the gazillion different models to give you an answer and sort of take a consensus. And that's a very different style of computation from fitting one precise model carefully. So I'll come back to that issue. Now I'm going to jump back a long time. Back in the mid-80s, people developed neural networks that have multiple laser feature detectors. And we had a learning algorithm called backpropagation that was
cues.zh: 也就是说，有人问你问题时，让无数模型都给出答案，然后取共识。这和仔细拟合一个精确模型是非常不同的计算方式。这个问题我稍后再回来说。现在跳回很久以前。80 年代中期，人们开发了具有多层特征检测器的神经网络。我们有一个学习算法叫反向传播，它

cues.en: at learning multiple layers of feature detectors. So you put some input in, run it through the net, compare that with what you wanted, then go backwards through the net using the chain rule to figure out how to change the weights on the incoming connections of each neuron. It was very exciting to begin with. It never worked very well for deep nets, except for Yann LeCun's deep nets, which used convolution. But for the other ones, it never worked very well. One problem with it was, back then, it was very hard to get very big sets of labeled data.
cues.zh: 能学习多层特征检测器。输入数据，过一遍网络，与期望结果比较，然后用链式法则反向穿过网络，算出如何改变每个神经元输入连接的权重。一开始非常令人兴奋。但它对深度网络一直效果不好，除了 Yann LeCun 使用卷积的深度网络。其他网络效果都不好。一个问题是，当时很难获得很大的标注数据集。

cues.en: You could get images or you get sine waves, but getting accurate labels for them was really tough. So we couldn't get enough labeled data. One solution, of course, has just worked very hard getting labeled data. And people in speech did that. They got big labeled data sets. Another solution is to say, let's see if we can learn most of the layers of feature detectors, maybe all but the last layer, by trying to model the input data, by trying to build a generative model of the sensory input, rather than by trying to
cues.zh: 你可以拿到图像或正弦波，但给它们准确标注真的很难。所以我们拿不到足够标注数据。一个办法当然是下苦功获取标注数据。语音领域的人就这么做，拿到了大型标注数据集。另一个办法是，看看能否通过建模输入数据、构建感官输入的生成模型，来学习大多数特征检测器层，也许除最后一层外，而不是试图

cues.en: decide what the right label for it is. And it turned out that approach worked quite well. So since 1985, a number of things have happened. Computers got a lot faster. That's the main thing that happened. Label data sets got a lot bigger. So now you can train big back propagation nets. We also found better ways to initialize the weights of these multi-layer nets by using unsupervised learning. And the combination of all three factors means that we can now initialize net sensibly.
cues.zh: 判断它的正确标签。结果这种方法效果相当好。自 1985 年以来发生了不少事。计算机快了很多，这是最主要的。标注数据集大了很多。所以现在可以训练大型反向传播网络。我们还找到了更好的方法，用无监督学习初始化这些多层网络的权重。这三个因素结合，意味着我们现在能合理地初始化网络。

cues.en: We can then turn them loose on a big data set. We initialize using unlabeled data, turn them loose on a big data set, and train the hell out of them with a big fast computer or a whole bunch of big fast computers. And they do very well. So here's some propaganda. Probably the most impressive application so far is in speech recognition. Some time ago, some of my students and me
cues.zh: 然后我们可以把它们放到大数据集上跑。我们用无标签数据初始化，把它们放到大数据集上，用一台大型快速计算机或一大堆大型快速计算机狠狠地训练它们。它们表现非常好。所以这里有点宣传意味。到目前为止，最令人印象深刻的应用可能是语音识别。前一段时间，我和我的一些学生

cues.en: but mainly my students, showed that on a relatively small data set of three hours of speech, there was a standard benchmark called TIMIT, we could beat the existing speaker-independent benchmarks by using a deep neural net to map from a window of acoustic frames to predictions about what pieces of what phoneme the middle frame was representing. So in speech, you use hidden Markov models to deal with temporal alignment.
cues.zh: 但主要是我的学生，展示了在相对较小的三小时语音数据集上，有一个叫 TIMIT 的标准基准，我们可以用深度神经网络把一窗声学帧映射为对中间帧代表哪个音素的哪个部分的预测，从而击败现有的说话人无关基准。所以在语音中，你用隐马尔可夫模型来处理时间对齐。

cues.en: For each phoneme, you have a hidden Markov model that has a few states, typically three. And sometimes for one phoneme, you have many different hidden Markov models, depending on what phoneme you think are beside it. But the problem is to get from the acoustic input to a prediction about how likely it is that it's this piece of this phoneme. And that's what the deep neural nets can do much better.
cues.zh: 对每个音素，你有一个隐马尔可夫模型，它有几个状态，通常是三个。有时对于一个音素，你会有许多不同的隐马尔可夫模型，取决于你认为它旁边是什么音素。但问题是要从声学输入得到预测：它是这个音素这一部分的概率有多大。而这正是深度神经网络能做得更好得多的事情。

cues.en: If you then feed those predictions to a decoder, which uses all sorts of knowledge about language and stuff, it gives you word strings that are more accurate than if you use the previous standard acoustic model. So here's some results from a recent review paper, which is notable because the paper has authors from MSR Research, IBM, and Google, as well as the University of Toronto. And this is on much bigger data sets.
cues.zh: 如果你把这些预测喂给解码器，解码器会使用各种关于语言之类的知识，它给出的词串会比使用之前的标准声学模型更准确。所以这里有一篇近期综述论文的一些结果，值得注意的是，这篇论文的作者来自 MSR Research、IBM、Google 以及多伦多大学。而且这是在更大的数据集上。

cues.en: MSR used quite a big data set of 309 hours. And they got the error rate on that data set down from 27% using the standard approach before these deep neural nets were applied to 18%. That's a huge improvement. And then on a different test set, they got it down for 23%, 16%. IBM, who probably had the best speech recognizer, the most carefully tuned one, on a somewhat smaller data set.
cues.zh: MSR 使用了一个相当大的 309 小时数据集。他们把这个数据集上的错误率从应用这些深度神经网络之前使用标准方法的 27% 降到了 18%。这是巨大的改进。然后在另一个测试集上，他们把它从 23% 降到了 16%。IBM 可能拥有最好的语音识别器，也就是调得最仔细的那个，在一个稍小的数据集上

cues.en: got their error rate of their very carefully tuned system down from 18.8% to 17.5%. And this was a very carefully tuned system. On Bing Voice Search, they got it down by a lot. Google used what Google thinks of as a small data set. And they got the error rate down to 12.3. They got it down to 12.3 from.
cues.zh: 把他们那个调得非常仔细的系统的错误率从 18.8% 降到了 17.5%。而这还是一个调得非常仔细的系统。在 Bing Voice Search 上，他们把它降了很多。Google 用了 Google 认为是小数据集的数据集。他们把错误率降到了 12.3。他们把它从

cues.en: 16%, which was trained on what they think of as a big data set. I don't know how big that is, but it was much bigger. So you give it much more data, it gets 16%. You give it less data, and you give it this deep neural net, and it gets 12%. And this is now down below 12%. And most of this progress was made by one summer intern, with a lot of help from the speech group, of course. And that's one of the best examples of deep neural nets doing something useful.
cues.zh: 16%，这个模型是在他们认为是大数据集的数据上训练出来的。我不知道那个有多大，但它大得多。所以你给它多得多的数据，它得到 16%。你给它更少的数据，再给它这个深度神经网络，它得到 12%。而现在这已经降到 12% 以下。大部分进展是由一个暑期实习生完成的，当然，语音组给了很多帮助。这是深度神经网络做出有用成果的最佳例子之一。

cues.en: announce that they're going to put their system, their deep neural net, live. OK, so the question is, is there anything we can't do with big, deep neural networks? Why aren't they the answer to everything? That's what we first thought when we did Backprop. I'm beginning to think it again. Well, here's one thing it's tricky to do. To train a big, deep neural network, you get a whole bunch of cores, and you split it over cores, and you run for a long time. And after you've used thousands of cores for several weeks,
cues.zh: 宣布他们要让自己的系统，也就是那个深度神经网络正式上线。好，那么问题来了：还有什么是大型深度神经网络做不了的吗？为什么它不能解决所有问题？当年我们刚搞出反向传播时就是这么想的，现在我又开始这么想了。不过，有件事确实很棘手。要训练一个大型深度神经网络，你需要弄来一大堆计算核心，把任务分散到这些核心上，跑很长时间。在耗费了几千个核心、跑了好几个星期之后，

cues.en: You've trained your great big network with, say, 1.7 billion parameters. And then someone says, hey, why don't you train 500 of those guys and average them? Well, that seems like hard work. But we know that averaging a whole bunch of models is always a big win. So if you want to win a machine learning competition like Netflix, what you should do is take lots of different models.
cues.zh: 你终于训练好了那个庞大的网络，比方说有 17 亿个参数。然后有人说：嘿，你为什么不训练 500 个这样的模型，把它们平均一下呢？呃，这听起来太费劲了。但我们知道，集成平均一大堆模型总是能带来巨大提升。所以如果你想赢下像 Netflix 这样的机器学习竞赛，你应该做的就是搞很多不同的模型。

cues.en: Throw away the ones that are no use, and keep the ones that work reasonably well, especially ones that are different from each other, and then average them. And so the winners were averaging more than 100 models. And we'd really like to do that with big, deep neural networks. That would presumably make them work better. And more evidence for that is you can take a rather wimpy machine learning method called decision trees. And one decision tree by itself doesn't work that well. But if you take a whole bunch of them, then they work really well.
cues.zh: 扔掉没用的，保留效果还可以的，尤其是彼此各不相同的模型，然后把它们做平均。当时的获胜者就平均了 100 多个模型。我们也很想在大型深度神经网络上这么做，理论上这能让它们效果更好。另一个佐证是，你可以看看决策树这种相当弱的机器学习方法。单棵决策树本身效果并不好，但如果你把一大堆决策树组合在一起，效果就会极佳。

cues.en: That's called random forests. And I believe the connect, the thing that gets you how you're dancing about from the 3D data, that's using random forests. And the point about decision trees is they're fast to train, and they're very fast at test time. So at test time, you can afford to average a whole bunch together, and also you can afford to train a whole bunch. And we would really like to do the same with these big, deep neural networks. On the face of it, that's going to be tricky.
cues.zh: 这就是所谓的随机森林。我相信 Kinect——就是那个能根据 3D 数据识别你跳舞动作的设备——用的就是随机森林。决策树的关键在于训练很快，而且在测试推理时也极快。因此在测试时，你完全能够承受把一大堆模型平均起来，训练时也负担得起。我们真的很想对这些大型深度神经网络做同样的事，但表面上看，这太难办了。

cues.en: So before I say how we're going to do that, let me just tell you two ways of averaging models. The most standard way is, if each model produces a probability distribution across classes, there's three classes here, what you do is simply average those probabilities. We shall give you a distribution that's softer than what the models predict and is guaranteed to be
cues.zh: 在讲我们打算怎么做之前，我先介绍两种模型平均的方法。最标准的做法是，如果每个模型都输出各个类别的概率分布（比如这里有三个类别），你直接对这些概率求平均即可。这会给你一个比单个模型预测更平滑的分布，并且必定……

cues.en: It's a better bet to use this average distribution than to pick one of the models at random. Of course, the best model might be better than your average. But when you've got a lot of models, it typically won't be. The other way we can combine distributions is to take a geometric mean instead of an arithmetic mean. We just multiply together the probabilities that the models give to the different classes. And then we take the nth root if we have n models. Then we get a bunch of numbers that don't add up to one. So we have to renormalize.
cues.zh: 使用这种平均分布，比随机挑一个模型靠谱得多。当然，表现最好的模型可能比平均值更好，但当模型数量很多时，通常不会这样。另一种组合分布的方法是计算几何平均，而不是算术平均。我们直接把各模型对不同类别给出的概率相乘，如果有 n 个模型就开 n 次方。这样得到的一组数值相加不等于 1，所以我们得重新归一化。

cues.en: But that also has the nice property that if you use this geometric mean, that will give you better predictions than picking a model at random. So here's the main idea of the talk. What we're going to do is we're going to take a slightly oversized neural net. And I'll begin with a neural net that just has one hidden layer. And each time I present some training data to it, I'm going to randomly emit each of the hidden units with a probability of 0.5.
cues.zh: 但这也有一个很好的性质：如果你使用这个几何平均，它给出的预测会比随机选一个模型更好。那么这就是本次演讲的核心思想。我们要做的是，取一个稍微大一点的神经网络。我先从一个只有一个隐藏层的神经网络讲起。每次我向它输入一些训练数据时，我会以 0.5 的概率随机丢弃每个隐藏单元。

cues.en: So you just pretend they're not there. So now we have a space of two to the n possible architectures, if there's n hidden units. So h to the h architectures is h hidden units. And we're sampling architectures from that space. So we're going to sample a whole bunch of different architectures. And each architecture is only ever going to see one training example. And it's only going to see it once, because the chance of sampling the same thing twice is negligible. And almost all the architectures will never be sampled. But all of these architectures are sharing the same weights, which is regularizing them a lot.
cues.zh: 所以你就当它们不存在。于是如果有 n 个隐藏单元，我们就有一个 2^n 种可能架构的空间。如果有 h 个隐藏单元，就是 2^h 种架构。我们从这个空间中采样架构。我们会采样一大堆不同的架构。每个架构只会看到过一个训练样本，而且只看到一次，因为两次采样到同一架构的概率可以忽略不计。几乎所有这些架构永远不会被采样到。但这些架构全都共享相同的权重，这会对它们起到很强的正则化作用。

cues.en: And so the question is, how well will this work? Also the question is, OK, you do that at training time. So when you're training, for each training example, you sample an architecture and then update the weights of the hidden units you're actually using slightly, then go to the next example. But what do you do at test time? Because how do you average all these things at test time? And it turns out if you're willing to take a geometric mean, that's very easy.
cues.zh: 那么问题就是，这效果会有多好？另一个问题是，好，你在训练时这么做。训练时，对每个训练样本，你采样一个架构，然后稍微更新你实际用到的隐藏单元的权重，再处理下一个样本。但测试时你该怎么做？因为测试时你怎么把所有这些平均起来？事实证明，如果你愿意取几何平均，那就非常容易。

cues.en: We can think of having this very large number of possible models. We've only trained a small fraction of them, but still a large number, as many as the number of presentations of the number of training examples. So you can think of that as very extreme bagging, where you're making your models different by giving them different training data and strongly regularizing them. And then at test time, what we can do is
cues.zh: 我们可以想象有数量极大的可能模型。我们只训练了其中一小部分，但仍然数量很大，和训练样本的呈现次数一样多。你可以把它看作非常极端的 bagging：通过给模型不同的训练数据并强烈正则化，使它们变得不同。然后在测试时，我们能做的是

cues.en: Because each hidden unit is there with a probability of a half during training, we make it be there all the time during test, but we halve its outgoing weights. So the expected contribution you get from it's the same. And now if you do that, when you have a softmax output group that's computing a probability distribution across classes, you can show that that exactly computes the geometric mean of the predictions of all these 2 to the h different networks.
cues.zh: 因为在训练时每个隐藏单元有一半的概率存在，我们在测试时让它一直存在，但把它的输出权重减半。这样你从它那里得到的期望贡献是一样的。现在如果你这么做，当你有一个 softmax 输出组在计算各类别上的概率分布时，可以证明它正好计算了这 2^h 个不同网络预测的几何平均。

cues.en: So that's a nice property. It means we just run this one mean network that's twice as big as any of the networks we run during training. And so for that factor of two, we can average all these networks together, including all the ones we didn't train. We're never trained, right. On the other hand, they're sharing weights with the ones that were trained. So even the ones that weren't trained are going to do sensible things, because there's massive weight sharing. So it's a funny kind of model averaging, where we combine model averaging with massive weight sharing.
cues.zh: 所以这是个很好的性质。这意味着我们只需运行这一个平均网络，它比训练时运行的任何网络都大一倍。于是用这个两倍的代价，我们可以把所有网络平均在一起，包括所有我们没训练过的网络。它们从未被训练过，对吧。另一方面，它们与训练过的网络共享权重。所以即使没训练过的网络也会做出合理的事情，因为有大量权重共享。所以这是一种有趣的模型平均，我们把模型平均和大量权重共享结合起来。

cues.en: If we have more hidden layers, we just use dropout and all of the hidden layers. And we always use, nearly always use 50% dropout because that's not a free parameter anymore. I mean, a half is sort of, it's not really a fudge, we just use a half. We've, of course, experimentally using different numbers. And any number between like 0.3 and 0.7 has very similar behavior. It's probably the case that if you have a very big net, if you can afford that,
cues.zh: 如果隐藏层较多，我们就在所有隐藏层上都应用 dropout。而且我们总是、或者说几乎总是使用 50% 的 dropout 率，因为这样它就不用作为一个自由参数来调了。我的意思是，选一半……这倒不算投机取巧，我们就是直接设为一半。当然，我们做实验测试过不同的数值。在 0.3 到 0.7 之间的任意数值，效果都非常相似。很可能的情况是，如果你有一个超大网络，而且算力允许的话，

cues.en: using much more dropout is better. That is keeping a smaller fraction on each case. If you have multiple hidden layers and you use 50% dropout in each layer, then when you use the mean net at test time, that's not the same as running all possible nets through an averaging them, taking the geometric mean. But it's a pretty good approximation to that. So you can do experiments where you run it stochastically a lot of times and average them. And you'll find you get something very similar.
cues.zh: 采用更高的 dropout 率效果会更好。也就是在每个样本上保留更少比例的神经元。如果有多个隐藏层，且每层都采用 50% 的 dropout，那么在测试时使用均值网络，并不等同于跑遍所有可能的网络再取其几何平均。但它是一个相当不错的近似。所以你可以做实验，随机跑很多次并取平均，你会发现得到的结果非常接近，

cues.en: to running the mean field net once. You can do the same thing in the input layer, and that also helps a lot. That's already being used by people in Yoshua Bengio's group and elsewhere, where you simply omit some of the inputs. So if it's an image, you just set some of the pixels to zero. And that acts as a good regularizer, but of course hurts you during training, but makes you generalize better. It's a good kind of noise to add. And this is just a generalization of that to all of the layers. In the input layer, you probably don't want to leave out half the pixels.
cues.zh: 几乎等同于直接跑一次平均场网络。你也可以在输入层做同样的操作，这也大有帮助。Yoshua Bengio 的团队以及其他研究人员已经在这么用了，也就是直接丢弃一部分输入。比如如果是图像，就把某些像素直接置零。这能起到很好的正则化效果，虽然在训练阶段会加大难度，但能让模型泛化得更好。这是一种有益的噪声。而这只是把这种做法推广到了所有层。在输入层，你可能并不想丢弃一半的像素。

cues.en: You want to leave out 20% of them or something. There is actually a familiar example of dropout, or a particular kind of dropout, for people who know about logistic regression. If you're doing logistic regression and you don't have enough data to fit your model really well, so you're prone to overfitting, what you can do is you can drop out all but one of the inputs. So now you're going to do logistic regression on just this model here and learn this weight. And you do that on a whole bunch of data.
cues.zh: 你可能只想丢掉 20% 左右。对于了解逻辑回归的人来说，其实有一个大家很熟悉的 dropout 例子，或者说是某种特殊的 dropout。做逻辑回归时，如果数据不够充分无法很好拟合模型，导致容易过拟合，你可以做的是：丢弃除了其中一个输入以外的所有输入。这样你就只对这一个输入特征做逻辑回归，并学习这个权重。然后你对整批数据都这么做。

cues.en: Focus on one, learn another way. If you do logistic regression like that, that's called Naive Bayes. At test time, you use all of these things together. If you want a distribution act, you really ought to take the geometric mean of what they all predict. But if you're just interested in the most likely class, you don't need to do that. And so Naive Bayes is actually an example of dropout, where you're using dropout to avoid overfitting. Of course, that immediately suggests that.
cues.zh: 专注这一个，学出另一个权重。如果像这样进行逻辑回归，它就叫作朴素贝叶斯。在测试时，你再把所有这些组合起来用。如果你需要精确的概率分布，确实应该对它们所有的预测取几何平均。但如果你只关心最可能的类别，就没必要这么麻烦。所以朴素贝叶斯其实就是 dropout 的一个例子，即通过 dropout 来避免过拟合。当然，这很自然地引出了一个想法：

cues.en: Why only consider the possibilities where you use them all, or you just use one of them? Why not consider sort of learning dropout rates for these guys using a validation set so that you're doing sort of subset selection, but probabilistic subset selection? And you're not going to say, I'm going to go for one particular subset of the features and try and find the best subset, which is what statisticians spend most of their time doing. You say, I'm going to have gazillions of subsets produced by giving each of these a probability that's not 0.5 anymore.
cues.zh: 为什么只考虑“要么全用、要么只挑一个”这两种极端情况呢？为什么不考虑用验证集来学习各个特征的 dropout 率，从而实现某种子集选择——即概率化的子集选择？你不再是说“我要选定某一个特定的特征子集并试图找到最优子集”，那是统计学家耗费大部分时间在做的事；而是说“我要通过给每个特征赋予不再是 0.5 的保留概率，来生成数不胜数的子集”。

cues.en: So that sort of useless features would have a low probability being included. Useful ones would have a much higher probability. And now you can average all those models together, and you'll get the big win out of model averaging. And that hasn't been, as far as I know, that's hardly been investigated, that kind of idea. So in a deep neural network, our experience is that if you take any deep neural network that's showing overfitting. So for example, in speech, any neural network that you stop early, because if you don't stop it early, it overfits. You can make it work.
cues.zh: 所以，那种无用特征被包含的概率会很低。有用特征的概率则会高得多。现在你可以把所有那些模型平均起来，就能从模型平均中获得很大收益。据我所知，这种想法几乎还没被研究过。所以在深度神经网络里，我们的经验是：拿任何一个表现出过拟合的深度神经网络。比如在语音任务里，任何早停的神经网络——因为不早停它就会过拟合。你可以让它工作起来。

cues.en: quite a lot better by using dropout. It works better than only stopping, and it causes a big decrease in the number of errors. People at Google say, yeah, but I don't have overfitting because I've got so much data. And the answer to that is, well, you should have overfitting, because you may have a lot of data, but that just means you should use a much bigger neural net. I mean, you can take the limit of infinite data, but I can take the limit of infinite computation. OK, so here's some initial experiments on a boring old task called MNIST, which is a kind of drosophila of machine learning.
cues.zh: 用 dropout 可以让它好很多。它比只做早停效果更好，并且会大幅减少错误数。Google 的人说：是啊，但我没有过拟合，因为我有海量数据。对此的回答是：嗯，你本来就该过拟合，因为你可能有很多数据，但这只说明你该用大得多的神经网络。我是说，你可以取无限数据的极限，而我可以取无限计算的极限。好，这里有一些关于一个无聊老任务 MNIST 的初步实验，它算是机器学习界的果蝇。

cues.en: And people say you shouldn't use MNIST because it's boring. And that's like telling a biologist, you shouldn't use Drosophila. So many biologists have used Drosophila. Why are you using Drosophila? Well, you're using Drosophila because so many other biologists use Drosophila. And you can compare things. A lot's known about it. So it's recognizing handwritten digits. And if you look on Yann LeCun's website, the best reported result for a kind of vanilla neural net is 160 errors on the test set. You can do much better than that.
cues.zh: 人们说你不该用 MNIST，因为它无聊。这就像告诉生物学家：你不该用果蝇。这么多生物学家都用过果蝇。你为什么用果蝇？嗯，你用果蝇是因为这么多其他生物学家都用果蝇。而且你可以比较各种东西。关于它已经知道很多。所以它是在识别手写数字。如果你看 Yann LeCun 的网站，一种普通神经网络报告的最好结果是测试集上 160 个错误。你可以比这好得多。

cues.en: by putting some knowledge in. You can put knowledge in either by making the net convolutional or by transforming the data using the fact that if you shift something, it stays the same class. So you can put knowledge in via messing with the data. And you can get down to about 25 errors now by doing all those tricks. But if you don't do that, if you do a form of learning that would still work if someone randomly permuted the pixels, then
cues.zh: 通过加入一些知识。你可以通过把网络做成卷积网络来加入知识，或者通过变换数据来加入知识，利用“平移某物后它仍是同一类别”这一事实。所以你可以通过折腾数据来加入知识。现在用所有这些技巧，可以把错误降到大约 25 个。但如果你不这么做，如果你采用一种即使有人随机打乱像素也仍然有效的学习方式，那么

cues.en: The best reported results 160 errors. That's this line here, this 160 errors. If you try various different neural nets, deep nets, so here's a net, the blue one, with 800 units in each layer. That's more than you'd normally use for MNIST and two hidden layers. And you train it with a big learning rate with a constraint on the weights so they don't blow up.
cues.zh: 报告的最好结果是 160 个错误。就是这里这条线，这个 160 个错误。如果你尝试各种不同的神经网络、深度网络，那么这里有一个网络，蓝色的那个，每层 800 个单元。这比通常用于 MNIST 的规模更大，而且有两个隐藏层。你用很大的学习率训练它，同时对权重加约束，免得它们爆炸。

cues.en: That already helps you do better than 160 errors, by the way. Then here's a whole bunch of different nets. And here's what happens if you train them with this big learning rate, and then you decay the learning rate. So you see they don't overfit. And they all do about the same. If you make the nets bigger and give them more layers, so this one has 1,200 units per layer and three layers. So that's much too big for normal kind of training. That would overfit horrendously.
cues.zh: 顺便说一句，这已经能让你做到比 160 个错误更好。然后这里有一大堆不同的网络。如果你用这么大的学习率训练它们，然后再衰减学习率，会发生什么。可以看到它们没有过拟合。它们的表现都差不多。如果你把网络做大、增加层数，比如这个每层有 1,200 个单元、共三层。那对常规训练来说太大了。那会严重过拟合。

cues.en: That one actually does really well. That gets down to just over 100 errors, which is really good performance on MNIST for a method that isn't being given extra information. So support vector machines get about 140 errors. They're back here on MNIST. And it was this gap between backprop and support vector machines that originally made people sort of switch to support vector machines. But now we've sort of reversed it. OK, but MNIST is a sort of boring task. To make this work, we do use weight constraints.
cues.zh: 那个网络实际上表现非常好。错误数降到略高于 100，对于没有额外信息的方法来说，在 MNIST 上已经是很不错的表现。支持向量机大约有 140 个错误。它们又回到 MNIST 这里了。正是反向传播和支持向量机之间的这个差距，最初让人们有点转向支持向量机。但现在我们某种程度上反过来了。不过 MNIST 是个有点无聊的任务。为了做到这一点，我们确实使用了权重约束。

cues.en: And if you're using L2 penalties on weights to keep them small, or L1 penalties to keep them small, it tends to work better to say, take each hidden unit and decide on the maximum length for the incoming weight vector using a validation set. And then during learning, if the weight vector is smaller than that, leave it alone. As soon as it hits that level, when it goes beyond that, then shrink it by division so it comes back to that maximum length.
cues.zh: 如果你用 L2 惩罚让权重保持较小，或者用 L1 惩罚让权重保持较小，通常更好的做法是：对每个隐藏单元，用验证集决定输入权重向量的最大长度。然后在学习过程中，如果权重向量小于这个长度，就别管它。一旦达到这个水平，当它超过时，就通过除法把它缩小，让它回到最大长度。

cues.en: That works quite a bit better than using L2 decay in the things we've tried. And that's what we're using here. It's just a hard constraint. But I can give you one way of thinking about it. When you do that division to normalize it back to the length, you'd stay at that length if you had Lagrange multipliers that were just right when you were doing your optimization. And those Lagrange multipliers are like the weight costs, the penalties on the weights.
cues.zh: 在我们试过的东西里，这比用 L2 衰减效果好不少。我们这里用的就是这个。它就是一个硬约束。不过我可以给你一种理解方式。当你做那个除法把它归一化回这个长度时，如果你优化时的拉格朗日乘子正好合适，你就会停在这个长度。那些拉格朗日乘子就像权重代价、对权重的惩罚。

cues.en: But these are penalties that change. So what will happen is, as the weights grow, when they're small, there's no penalty. Once they hit the constraint, then if some of the weights want to grow a lot and the others of the weights don't want to grow much, you have to put in big Lagrange multipliers, and that'll actually push the ones that want to grow back down to a zero. So in effect, the L2 penalty on each connection adapts to how much the other connections want to change. Yeah. OK.
cues.zh: 但这些惩罚是会变化的。所以会发生的是，随着权重增长，当它们很小时，没有惩罚。一旦碰到约束，如果一些权重想大幅增长，而另一些权重不想增长太多，你就必须加入很大的拉格朗日乘子，这实际上会把那些想增长的权重压回到零。所以实际上，每条连接上的 L2 惩罚会适应其他连接想改变的程度。是的。好。

cues.en: So here's experiments on Timmy, which was more interesting. You train the neural network on a window of acoustic frames. You're trying to predict which states and which HMMs the central frame corresponds to. With standard fine-tuning, you get 22.7% after doing this unsupervised pre-training. And that's already a very good result.
cues.zh: 所以这是在 Timmy 上的实验，更有意思。你在一个声学帧窗口上训练神经网络。你要预测中心帧对应哪些状态和哪些 HMM。经过这种无监督预训练后，用标准微调能得到 22.7%。这已经是非常好的结果。

cues.en: We can do better than that, but what we did was we went to a different way of pre-processing the data, so we hadn't already overfitted it a lot. We're using Dampov-Iskaldi system for this, and that was sort of the first time we'd used it. Then when you take this net and apply dropout, you get down to 19.7, which is a record for speaker-independent methods. That's a big drop. So here's, that's the phone error rate. You can also look at, as you're training,
cues.zh: 我们可以做得更好，但我们的做法是改用另一种数据预处理方式，这样就不会已经严重过拟合。我们用了 Dampov-Iskaldi 系统来做这件事，那算是我们第一次使用它。然后，拿这个网络并应用 dropout，错误率降到 19.7，这是说话人无关方法的一个记录。这是很大的下降。这就是音素错误率。你还可以看，在训练过程中，

cues.en: You can look at how well you're classifying the individual frames, which is called the classification rate. And the classification error rate, if you just do normal fine-tuning where you're not doing dropout, you see it comes down and then it overfits. And so early stopping, if you could stop at just the right point, will get you one of these points for these different nets. With dropout, it comes down and it just keeps going down.
cues.zh: 你可以看单个帧分类得有多好，这称为分类率。而分类错误率，如果你只做普通微调、不用 dropout，你会看到它先下降，然后过拟合。所以早停，如果你能在恰当的点停下来，就能为不同网络得到这些点中的一个。用 dropout 时，它下降后还会一直下降。

cues.en: If you look at the cross entropy error here, the classification rate doesn't go up. The cross entropy error goes up very slightly. But basically, it's hardly overfitting at all. And all these different architectures do very similar, and all much better than what you would get with early stopping. So if you're using early stopping, stop. Just to show it was universal, we thought we'd do document classification. It didn't work so well for that, but it worked. So we took what we think of as a big document set of the order of a million documents.
cues.zh: 如果你看这里的交叉熵误差，分类率并没有上升。交叉熵误差只是非常轻微地上升。但基本上，它几乎完全没有过拟合。所有这些不同架构表现都很相似，而且都比你用早停得到的结果好得多。所以如果你在用早停，那就停下吧。为了证明它具有通用性，我们想做个文档分类。它在这方面效果没那么好，但确实有效。于是我们用一个我们认为是大型文档集的数据，大约一百万篇文档。

cues.en: which are represented by the counts of the 2,000 most frequent words. There's a sort of little hierarchy of classes. We simplified it by taking 50 non-overlapping classes. That's sort of the second level of the hierarchy. We removed one class that accounted for about a third of the data, and we removed a few classes that hardly had any representatives. So then we had data that had 50 classes, and we could see how well Dropout helped. And if you train with that Dropout,
cues.zh: 这些文档用出现最频繁的 2,000 个词的计数来表示。类别有一种小的层级结构。我们把它简化成 50 个互不重叠的类别。那大概是层级的第二层。我们移除了一个约占三分之一数据的类别，还移除了几个几乎没有样本的类别。于是我们得到有 50 个类别的数据，就能看出 Dropout 帮助有多大。而如果你用 dropout 训练，

cues.en: You get your classic kind of thing that will favor early stopping. And with dropout, you get sort of a percent or two better. And you don't overfit. So for document classification, it works. It's not as big a win as for the other things. But in general, our experience is pick a task at random. And this will give you 5% to 10% less errors just by using a somewhat bigger net and using dropout. Here's a more interesting task. This is classifying color images. They're small color images.
cues.zh: 你会得到那种典型情况，会倾向于早停。而用 dropout，你能好个百分之一到二。而且不会过拟合。所以对文档分类，它是有效的。它不像其他任务那样提升巨大。但总的来说，我们的经验是随便挑一个任务。只要用稍大一点的网络并使用 dropout，就能让错误减少 5% 到 10%。这里有个更有意思的任务。这是对彩色图像分类。它们是小尺寸彩色图像。

cues.en: So I designed this task to be as similar as possible to MNIST, but nevertheless to use real images from the web. So there are 32 by 32 color images. There's 10 different classes. These are examples in the test set of birds. So the images are produced in the following way. First, search the web for bird and things that come under bird in some net of classes.
cues.zh: 所以我设计这个任务，尽可能与 MNIST 相似，但仍然使用来自网络的真实图像。所以是 32×32 的彩色图像。有 10 个不同类别。这些是测试集中鸟类的例子。图像是这样生成的。首先，在网上搜索 bird，以及某个类别网络中归在 bird 下的东西。

cues.en: Then take all those things and give them to Toronto undergraduates and say, the instructors are roughly this. Is the one dominant thing in the image, and could that plausibly have the label BERT? You discover after a while that you're paying these undergraduates, and they're actually playing games with each other on their laptops and not labeling images, because labeling images is incredibly boring.
cues.zh: 然后把这些东西全交给多伦多本科生，跟他们说，指导语大致是这样。图像里是否有一个占主导的东西，它是否可能被标成 BERT？过一阵你会发现，你付钱给这些本科生，他们实际上却在笔记本电脑上互相玩游戏，不给图像打标签，因为给图像打标签实在太无聊了。

cues.en: The only person I've ever found who liked labeling images was Radford Neil's daughter, who would look at a display of 100 images and go, cat, cat. I think she was about two at the time. And so image labelers ought to be age two. They really get into it. They would probably pay you to do it. So Alex Krzyzewski trained a great big neural net, which is convolutional. He tried lots of things. His best net was getting about 18% error, which is about the record on this.
cues.zh: 我见过的唯一喜欢给图像打标签的人，是 Radford Neil 的女儿。她会看着一屏100张图，然后说：猫，猫。我想她当时大概两岁。所以图像标注员就该是两岁小孩。他们是真的投入。他们可能还会付钱给你来做。于是 Alex Krzyzewski 训练了一个很大的神经网络，是卷积网络。他试了很多东西。他最好的网络错误率约18%，这差不多是这个任务的纪录。

cues.en: He then got that down to 16% error. He's now got that much lower by using translations of the images and things. But if you don't cheat, if you don't use transformed data where you put in extra knowledge, that's quite a big win. These numbers are always changing because it keeps improving things. Here's a more serious test of object recognition. So I got fed up with the computer vision people saying that
cues.zh: 后来他把错误率降到16%。现在他通过使用图像平移之类的方法，把错误率降得低多了。但如果你不作弊，不使用加入额外知识的变换数据，这已经是很大的提升了。这些数字一直在变，因为不断有人在改进。下面是一个更严肃的物体识别测试。我受够了计算机视觉领域的人总说：

cues.en: You neural net guys are just trying simple sets like Caltech 101. So I called up Malik, and I said, who has been saying that deep neural nets haven't really proved themselves for object recognition, because they're always using things that are too simple. So I talked to Jitendra, and Jitendra agreed that if we could work on ImageNet, then that was a real result. ImageNet would be impressive if we could make it work on ImageNet.
cues.zh: 你们搞神经网络的人只是在试 Caltech 101 这种简单数据集。于是我给 Malik 打电话，我说，是谁一直在说深度神经网络在物体识别上还没有真正证明自己，因为它们总是用太简单的东西。所以我和 Jitendra 谈了，他同意，如果我们能在 ImageNet 上做，那才算真正结果。如果我们能让它在 ImageNet 上跑通，那才会令人印象深刻。

cues.en: There's a 2010 competition where they disclosed the test set. So you can try it yourself. It's got 1.3 million training images. So 1,000 different classes. You're having to do 1,000-way classification. You've got about 1,000 examples of each class. So it's going to be really important to share features. The winner of the 2010 competition got 47% error for their first choice.
cues.zh: 2010年有个比赛，他们公开了测试集。所以你可以自己试。它有130万张训练图像，1000个不同类别。你得做1000类分类。每个类别大约有1000个样本。所以共享特征会非常重要。2010年比赛的冠军首选答案错误率是47%。

cues.en: If you say it's OK to get in your top five choices, then they got 25% error. So that was the state of the art in 2010. The state of the art now is a little bit better. They're down to 45%. So there's another competition. The winner of that competition went back to this competition and showed that they get 45% on this competition. So the state of the art, as far as we know, is 45% on this. Alex tried a whole bunch of neural nets.
cues.zh: 如果规则是前五个选项里命中就算对，那他们的错误率是25%。这就是2010年的最先进水平。现在的最先进水平稍微好一点，已经降到45%。后来又有另一个比赛。那个比赛的赢家又回到这个比赛，证明他们在这个比赛上能达到45%。所以据我们所知，这个比赛的最先进水平是45%。Alex 试了一大堆神经网络。

cues.en: He ended up with seven hidden layers not counting the max pooling layer. The only layers were convolutional, so they didn't have too many parameters. The later layers were fully connected, so they had lots of parameters. They had like 4,000 units fully connected, so that's 16 million parameters right there. And there's two of them. He used this trick of transforming the training data. So he reduced the images to 256 by 256.
cues.zh: 他最终用了七个隐藏层，不算最大池化层。这些层只有卷积层，所以参数不太多。后面的层是全连接层，所以参数很多。全连接层大约有 4,000 个单元，光那里就有 1600 万个参数。而且有两个这样的层。他用了变换训练数据的技巧，把图像缩小到 256×256。

cues.en: But then didn't use all of that image. He used patches that were a bit smaller. So he got lots of different patches. So he was getting things in lots of different faces. So he never had the same training example twice. And he used a bunch of other tricks that I didn't try to go into and aren't sort of relevant to the effect of dropout. So he got down to about 48% error. So about the state of the art using all these methods. But then.
cues.zh: 但并没有用整张图像。他用的是稍小一些的图像块，因此得到很多不同的图像块，也就以很多不同面貌看到目标。所以他从未两次遇到同一个训练样本。他还用了一堆其他技巧，我没打算细讲，而且这些技巧和 dropout 的效果没多大关系。这样他把错误率降到了约 48%，差不多是当时用上所有这些方法后的最好水平。但接下来。

cues.en: He applied dropout to the globally connected layers. And he's now down to 39% error for the best one and 19% error for the top five. And that's a huge improvement. I mean, people who do computer vision will tell you that's a big step forward. Here's some samples from Alex's net. This is before he was getting his very best results. So this is a slightly worse version of his net. But just to show you what this task is like.
cues.zh: 他把 dropout 用在全连接层上。现在最好的结果错误率降到 39%，前五错误率降到 19%。这是巨大的提升。我是说，做计算机视觉的人会告诉你，这是很大的进步。这里有一些 Alex 网络的样本。这是在他取得最佳结果之前，所以这是他网络稍差一点的版本。只是为了让你看看这个任务是什么样。

cues.en: You're given a picture like that, and you have to say which of a thousand things it is. And Alex's neural net says it's an otter. Now, I'm actually an apologist for deep neural nets. So I think an otter is a jolly good thing to say, because notice you haven't got the tip of the beak, and you've got the wet fur of an otter here. And I think it's very clever to recognize the wet fur of an otter. It does get quail second, and it does get all the things that I can't distinguish from an quail like a rough grouse and a partridge after that.
cues.zh: 给你一张这样的图片，你要说出它是上千类中的哪一类。Alex 的神经网络说它是水獭。其实我是深度神经网络的辩护者，所以我觉得说水獭是个相当不错的答案，因为注意你没看到鸟喙的尖端，而这里有水獭湿漉漉的毛皮。我认为能认出这是水獭的湿毛皮非常聪明。它确实把鹌鹑排在第二，后面也确实列出了我分不清是不是鹌鹑的东西，比如毛腿松鸡和山鹑。

cues.en: This one is obviously a snow plow. And then you look at its errors. The errors are always more informative. Sort of drilling platform and garbage truck seem fine. Why does it think it's a lifeboat? Well, this might not be snow. It might be sort of foamy water. And if you look again, here's the flag at the front of the lifeboat. Here's the flag at the back of the lifeboat. Here's the bridge of the lifeboat. It really does look very like a lifeboat.
cues.zh: 这个显然是扫雪车。然后你看看它的错误。错误总是更有信息量。钻井平台和垃圾车之类看起来还行。为什么它认为是救生艇？嗯，这可能不是雪，可能是某种泛着泡沫的水。再看一眼，这里是救生艇前部的旗子，这里是救生艇后部的旗子，这里是救生艇的舰桥。它看起来确实非常像救生艇。

cues.en: Like I say, I'm an apologist for neural nets. This one, it gets completely wrong, OK? It doesn't get in the top five. The right answer is scabbard. It's bizarre. It says earthworm. Guillotine, you can see why it says guillotine, two big vertical bits. This is presumably something to do with color and the forest. Broom, you can see why it says broom. But earthworm, why does it say earthworm? But if you look in a bit more detail, you can see a couple of earthworms here.
cues.zh: 就像我说的，我是神经网络的辩护者。这个它完全搞错了，好吧？它没进前五。正确答案是刀鞘。真奇怪。它说是蚯蚓。断头台，你能明白它为什么说断头台，两个大的竖直部分。这大概和颜色以及森林有关。扫帚，你能明白它为什么说扫帚。但蚯蚓，它为什么说蚯蚓？不过如果你看得更仔细一点，你能在这里看到几条蚯蚓。

cues.en: Now, you may think this is just fantasy, but what Alex can do is he can back propagate from the class label to say, tell me which pixels are having the most effect on your confidence in this class label. So he can see the sensitivity of the label to the pixels. He hasn't done it with this one, but there's one where the object is a mite, which is very small in the image. There's a leaf with a mite, and it's to one side in the image. If you back propagate there.
cues.zh: 现在，你可能觉得这纯属幻想，但 Alex 能做的是，他可以从类别标签反向传播，问：告诉我哪些像素对你判定这个类别标签的置信度影响最大。这样他就能看到标签对像素的敏感度。这张图他没这么做，但有一张图里目标是一只螨虫，在图像中非常小。有一片叶子上面有只螨虫，它在图像的一侧。如果你在那里反向传播。

cues.en: It's the pixels of the mite that are causing it to say mite. So this isn't just totally fantasy. I enjoy showing these, so let's show some more. ImageNet has a wide variety of classes of things, and you can see why they allow you to get it in the top five. So what's the right answer here? Well, I would have said probably microwave, if not microwave dishwasher, if that's what that is. That's exactly what it says.
cues.zh: 正是螨虫的那些像素让它说是螨虫。所以这并不完全是幻想。我喜欢展示这些，所以再看一些。ImageNet 有种类繁多的类别，你能明白为什么它们允许你把它算进前五。那么这里正确答案是什么？嗯，我本来会说大概是微波炉，如果不是微波炉，那就是洗碗机，如果那东西是洗碗机的话。它说的正是这个。

cues.en: The right answer is electric range. I don't even know where the electric range is. I think it must be over here. Or it might just be, you know, there must be one there. Because where there's a dishwasher and a microwave, there must be an electric range. And there's a wash basin. So the right answer there is very dubious. And it actually gave better answers. Incidentally, if the test set has some answers that aren't the best answers, and if you got them all right, that would be zero error. But if you give better answers in a test set, that's got to be negative error.
cues.zh: 正确答案是电炉灶。我甚至不知道电炉灶在哪里。我想它一定在这边。或者它可能只是，你知道，那里肯定有一个。因为哪里有洗碗机和微波炉，哪里就一定有电炉灶。还有一个洗手盆。所以那里的正确答案非常可疑。而它实际上给出了更好的答案。顺便说，如果测试集里有些答案不是最佳答案，而你把它们全答对了，那就是零误差。但如果你在测试集里给出更好的答案，那就得是负误差。

cues.en: So my aim is to get this thing giving negative error rate. It has distributed things like turnstiles that it can recognize. It has things from catalogs, like bulletproof vests. Here's my favorite error. You show it some iPhone headphones, and it says it's a corkscrew or lipstick or a screw. And then it says ant. Why on earth would it think they're an ant? But if you look at it.
cues.zh: 所以我的目标是让这个东西给出负错误率。它能识别像旋转闸机这样分布在各处的东西。它还有商品目录里的东西，比如防弹背心。这是我最喜欢的错误。你给它看一些 iPhone 耳机，它说这是开瓶器、口红或螺丝。然后它说是蚂蚁。它到底为什么会觉得它们是蚂蚁？但如果你看看它。

cues.en: This is the view you don't want to have of an ant. It's an enormous ant. And it's just about to bite you. It's looking down on you. Here's some tenny. This is an aphid's view of an ant. Now, we can't prove that that's why it said ant. But why else would it say ant? There's another way to think about dropout. So I've shown you dropout works. Another way to think about it, which is like what the evolutionary theorists think.
cues.zh: 这是你不想看到的蚂蚁视角。它是一只巨大的蚂蚁。它正要咬你。它正俯视着你。这里有个很小的版本。这是蚜虫眼中的蚂蚁。现在，我们无法证明这就是它说蚂蚁的原因。但它还能因为什么说蚂蚁呢？还有另一种理解 dropout 的方式。我已经向你展示了 dropout 有效。另一种理解方式，类似于进化理论家的想法。

cues.en: is that rather than think of it in terms of model averaging, think of it in terms of what a hidden unit has to do. So a hidden unit in a net would like to do something useful. If he knows exactly who he's going to be collaborating with, then he can sort of tune what he does to what he can expect them to be doing, and you get these complex co-adaptations. But if you don't know who else is going to be there, you're out of luck if you try and tune to them. You better do something that's sort of individually useful.
cues.zh: 与其从模型平均的角度考虑，不如从隐藏单元必须做什么的角度考虑。所以网络中的一个隐藏单元会想做点有用的事。如果它确切知道要跟谁协作，那它就能把自己做的事调整到它预期对方会做的事，于是你就得到这些复杂的协同适应。但如果你不知道还有谁会在那里，你还想调整去适应它们，那就没戏了。你最好做点单独来看有用的事。

cues.en: It turns hidden units into rugged individualists. Except that, their rugged individualists would like to do something that's useful given what the other guys are up to in general. So given all these combinatorially many sets of other guys you might have to work with, do something that's generally helpful. And that will cause you to do something different from what they're doing, but not relying on which particular ones are there. And that makes you far more robust against them changing, but also against the environment changing.
cues.zh: 它把隐藏单元变成了坚定的个人主义者。只不过，这些个人主义者在考虑其他人在做什么的大体情况下，也希望能做点有用的事。也就是说，面对可能需要合作的各种排列组合的同伴，要去做普遍有帮助的事。这促使你做一些和他们不同的事，同时又不依赖具体有谁在场。这不仅让你对同伴的变动更加鲁棒，也对环境的变化更加鲁棒。

cues.en: And being robust against the environment changing is what prevents overfitting. In machine learning, the environment changes when you switch from the training set to the test set. And what you really want to be robust against is those changes. So here's a little example of that. Here's two training cases. Those are the inputs, and those are the desired outputs. And here's a set of weights that does perfectly fine. You see 5 plus 11 gives you 6. And if you add in these, you get 4.
cues.zh: 而对环境变化保持鲁棒，正是防止过拟合的关键。在机器学习中，从训练集切换到测试集就是环境变化。你真正想要抵御的，正是这类变化。这里有个小例子。这是两个训练样本。那些是输入，那些是期望输出。这里有一组权重表现得相当不错。你看，5 加上 11 得到 6。如果把这些加进去，就得到 4。

cues.en: But the 5 and 11 are co-adapted. This minus 5 is going in the wrong direction, and it's relying on this plus 11 being there. Otherwise, it's saying something really stupid. If you do dropout, and this plus 11 sometimes isn't there, you'll see that this minus 5 is a really bad idea. If you do dropout, you'll get weights more like this. Actually, you'll get weights of twice this, but when you put them into the mean net, you halve them, and then you get weights like this. And then these weights will work.
cues.zh: 但 5 和 11 发生了共适应。这个 -5 走错了方向，它完全依赖于 +11 的存在。否则，它的输出就很离谱。如果用 dropout，而这个 +11 有时不在，你就会发现这个 -5 是个极差的主意。用了 dropout 之后，得到的权重会更像这样。实际上得到的权重是这个的两倍，但放进平均网络时会减半，然后就会得到像这样的权重。这样这些权重就能正常工作了。

cues.en: In machine learning, there's sort of two ways of regularizing things. One is model averaging, and the other is adding noise. People have shown that adding Gaussian noise to weights in a linear system is exactly equivalent to an L2 penalty. Actually, adding Gaussian noise to the inputs is exactly equivalent to an L2 penalty, sorry. Yeah, Gaussian noise to the inputs, that's like having an L2 penalty. As you have a more complex net, it gets a bit more complicated. But people generally think of adding noise as different from doing model averaging.
cues.zh: 在机器学习中，正则化大概有两种方法。一种是模型平均，另一种是添加噪声。有人已经证明，在线性系统中给权重添加高斯噪声完全等价于 L2 惩罚。抱歉，实际上是给输入添加高斯噪声完全等价于 L2 惩罚。没错，给输入加高斯噪声，就相当于施加 L2 惩罚。网络变得更复杂时，情况也会更复杂一些。但人们通常认为添加噪声和做模型平均是两码事。

cues.en: What dropout shows is it's a case when you can view it either as adding noise or as model averaging. They're not really different methods. I want to go into one more advantage of using dropout, which goes back to evolutionary biology, I guess. When you train a net with dropout, the neurons are very robust against their co-workers changing. They don't know who's going to be there. And so they better do something that's robust against these changes.
cues.zh: 但 dropout 表明，它既可以被看作添加噪声，也可以被看作模型平均。它们本质上并不是不同的方法。我还想讲讲使用 dropout 的另一个优势，我想这可以追溯到进化生物学。用 dropout 训练网络时，神经元对同伴的变动具有极高的鲁棒性。它们不知道谁会在场。因此它们最好做一些对这些变化保持鲁棒的事情。

cues.en: That means these nets ought to be very good in genetic algorithms. You ought to be able to take two different nets and take, let's suppose you just have one hidden net. Take half the hidden units from one net and half the hidden units from the other net. Already these hidden units are robust against their coworkers changing. So when you take half from each net, you'll get something that doesn't work properly yet.
cues.zh: 这意味着这些网络应该很适合遗传算法。你应当能取两个不同的网络，假设你只有一个隐藏网络。从一个网络取一半隐藏单元，从另一个网络取一半隐藏单元。这些隐藏单元已经能抵抗同伴的变化。所以当你从每个网络各取一半时，得到的东西还不能正常工作。

cues.en: But it already works pretty well. And then you said Skiva has tested this. It works pretty well. And then a little bit of training, and it works almost as well as the parents. So now what you can do is you can take a big cluster, or a big farm, and you can do a lot of computation with almost no communication. So you're running lots of networks on a little bunch of local cores. And every so often,
cues.zh: 但它已经工作得挺好了。然后你说 Skiva 测试过这个。它效果很好。再训练一点点，它就几乎和父代一样好。所以现在你可以做的是，拿一个大集群或大农场，做大量计算而几乎不需要通信。于是你在一小批本地核心上运行很多网络。而且每隔一段时间，

cues.en: One of these networks advertises for a mate. She considers the possibilities, chooses one, and then you get half the hidden units from the mother and half from the father. The mother network then gets suspended. Mothers know about this. And that core is used to run the child network. The child network then does some more training. And then you make a prediction about who's going to end up best, the mother.
cues.zh: 其中一个网络会公开求偶。她考虑各种可能，选一个，然后你从母亲那里取一半隐藏单元，从父亲那里取一半。母亲网络随后被挂起。母亲们知道这件事。那个核心被用来运行子代网络。子代网络再做更多训练。然后你预测谁最终会表现最好，是母亲。

cues.en: or this child. The child may not yet be as good as a mother because it hasn't finished training, but you have to make some prediction. Is this child likely to end up better than the mother? If so, you kill the mother. If not, you kill the child. You may ask, what happens to the fathers? Well, it's very important in this algorithm to have rapid gender changes. So a network, there's a father one time, better be a mother another time. If you're a father, you never get killed. And so to get rid of them, you have to do a gender change.
cues.zh: 还是这个子代。子代可能还没母亲那么好，因为它还没训练完，但你必须做某种预测。这个子代最终有可能比母亲更好吗？如果会，就杀掉母亲。如果不会，就杀掉子代。你可能会问，父亲们会怎样？这个算法里快速切换性别非常重要。所以一个网络，这次是父亲，下次最好当母亲。如果你是父亲，你永远不会被杀。所以要淘汰它们，就得做一次性别变换。

cues.en: Yeah. Indeed. One is just sort of standard dropout again. One wouldn't work so well. It may well be that in biology you have two, because organizing group sex is too complicated. But I don't know. We haven't done the experiments. We just had one very preliminary experiment to show that if you make two of these things, you get a child that quickly learns to be good.
cues.zh: 对。确实。一个就又是那种标准 dropout。只有一个效果不会那么好。生物学里有两个，很可能是因为组织群体交配太复杂了。但我不知道。我们还没做实验。我们只做了一个非常初步的实验，表明如果你做两个这种东西，得到的子代能很快学会变好。

cues.en: So the robustness you get from dropout is really helpful. And the thing about genetic algorithms is you can use a million of your spare cores, and you can be using them sort of fully with hardly any communication. Now for something that's not completely different. If you think what dropout is doing, it's taking a neuron, and the neuron is a logistic neuron in my nets. So it computes a probability p. And then it computes a number p from the logistic.
cues.zh: 所以 dropout 带来的鲁棒性真的很有用。遗传算法的一点是，你可以用上百万个空闲核心，并且几乎不用通信就能把它们差不多充分利用起来。现在讲点并非完全不同的事。想想 dropout 在做什么：它取一个神经元，而我的网络里这个神经元是 logistic 神经元。它计算一个概率 p。然后从 logistic 计算出一个数 p。

cues.en: That's the output of the logistic, which we call the neural activity. It then sends this number, this real value, with a probability of 0.5 to the layer above. That's what dropout's doing. Well, that has exactly the same expected value as sending a 0.5 with a probability of p. The variance is slightly different. So why not try that? So take a neural net.
cues.zh: 这就是 logistic 函数的输出，也就是我们所说的神经元活动。然后它以 0.5 的概率将这个数值、这个实数传给上一层。这就是 dropout 的机制。而这与以概率 p 发送 0.5 的期望值完全一样。只是方差略有不同。那为什么不试试看呢？拿一个神经网络来说。

cues.en: When we pre-trained these neural nets, we used stochastic binary neurons anyway. And instead of doing back propagation by sending these real values, why not just send a single bit chosen stochastically? So you compute p, and then with probability p, you send a 1. It's sort of bizarre, because we always thought that the breakthrough in back propagation was realizing that you needed to send those
cues.zh: 当我们对这些神经网络做预训练时，反正用的也是随机二值神经元。那与其在反向传播中传递这些实数值，为什么不直接随机传递一个 bit 呢？先算出 p，再以概率 p 发送一个 1。这听上去挺不可思议的，因为我们过去总觉得反向传播的突破就在于意识到必须传递那些

cues.en: real numbers. Actually, if you do that, it works really well. The neural net is obviously slower to learn. And you need to make it a bit bigger to be able to learn the same amount of stuff. But it generalizes much better. And from preliminary experiments I've done, the improvement you get in performance is similar to what you get from dropout. So what this is saying is, if you've got a big, deep neural net, and you're relying on
cues.zh: 实数。但实际上真这样做的话，效果非常不错。神经网络的学习速度显然会变慢。而且为了学到同等量的信息，你得把网络做得稍大一点。但它的泛化能力要好得多。根据我做的初步实验，它带来的性能提升与 dropout 相当。所以这说明，如果你有一个庞大的深度神经网络，并且依靠

cues.en: Regularizing it is big, right? It doesn't have enough training data. You want to regularize it by using something like dropout or noise. It's actually better for the neurons to send a single bit than it is for them to send an analog value. In dropout, your variance, if you send a half, if you send p with probability of half, your average value is a half p. And so your value is going to be a quarter p away from that.
cues.zh: 正则化来约束它——毕竟网络很大，对吧？训练数据不够用。你想用类似 dropout 或噪声的方法来进行正则化。其实神经元传递单个 bit，比传递模拟连续值效果更好。在 dropout 中，关于方差，如果以二分之一的概率发送 p，你的均值就是 0.5p。所以数值与均值的偏差……

cues.en: Whatever. That's the variance you get with a stochastic bit, but where you're sending a 0.5. This is the variance. You can see that when p equals a half, they're the same. That's good, because they have to be. When p is big, this guy has lower variance than this guy. But when p is small, this guy has bigger variance. This guy, when p is small, he goes as p squared. This guy goes as p.
cues.zh: 算了吧。这就是随机 bit 得到的方差，不过发送的是 0.5。这就是方差。可以看出，当 p 等于 0.5 时它们相等。这很好，因为本来就该一样。当 p 较大时，后者的方差比前者小。但当 p 较小时，后者的方差更大。在 p 很小时，这个呈 p 平方的趋势，而那个呈 p 的趋势。

cues.en: P is small. Using a SCASI bit, you're getting even more variance than you do with dropout. And that's the Poisson limit when P is small. You ignore this term, and the variance is proportional to P now. And that's roughly what neurons are like. A lot of neuroscientists will tell you what a neuron does is it computes a Poisson rate, and then it emits spikes according to a Poisson. You have to take into account the fact that it can't immediately emit another spike, and that makes life more complicated. But ignoring that,
cues.zh: p 很小。使用随机 bit 时，你得到的方差甚至比 dropout 还要大。这就是 p 很小情况下的泊松极限。忽略这一项，方差现在就正比于 p 了。真实神经元大致也是如此。很多神经科学家会告诉你，神经元所做的就是计算泊松发放率，然后按照泊松分布发放脉冲。当然必须考虑它不能马上发放下一记脉冲，这让情况更复杂。但抛开这点，

cues.en: A Poisson model is a pretty good model of a neuron. And it's always been a puzzle. Why don't they use the times of spikes? Why do they do all this randomness? And the answer is because that's what they want to do. That's the right thing to do if you want to fit models to data. If you sent real numbers, you'd do worse. So here's an amusing piece of history, which I already alluded to. When we first discovered that you can train lots of layers of features unsupervised, we're using things called Boltz machines as stochastic binary units.
cues.zh: 泊松模型是对神经元相当不错的模拟。这过去一直是个谜：为什么它们不利用脉冲发放的时间点？为什么搞这么多随机性？答案是，因为这正是其目的所在。如果你想让模型去拟合数据，这么做才对。如果传递实数，表现反而更差。这里有一段有趣的历史，我刚才也提到过。当我们最初发现可以无监督地训练多层特征时，使用的就是被称为玻尔兹曼机、带有随机二值单元的模型。

cues.en: Terry Sinofsky insisted on stochastic binary units in 1980, when I first met him, because he said that's what neurons are like. And so we tried to develop ways of computing with them, because that's what neurons are like. We discovered we could train loads of feature techniques like this, but after doing that, we knew backpropagation was good for fine tuning, so we pretended they were deterministic neurons, which was a horrible intellectual fudge, and we used backpropagation. It turns out...
cues.zh: Terry Sinofsky 在 1980 年我第一次见他时，坚持要用随机二值单元，因为他说神经元就是这样。于是我们试着开发用它们计算的方法，因为神经元就是这样。我们发现可以用这种方式训练大量特征检测器之类的技术，但做完之后我们知道反向传播很适合微调，所以就假装它们是确定性神经元——这是一次糟糕的智力糊弄——然后用了反向传播。结果发现……

cues.en: If you don't do that, if you keep running the mysticastic binary neurons in the forward pass, but run the standard back propagation in the backward pass. So in the backward pass, you're using those p's and 1 minus p's, but they never need to be communicated outside the neuron. Then it actually trains slower, but it generalizes much better. So it's a better thing to do. And so I want to end with some explanations of why cortical neurons don't send analog values.
cues.zh: 如果你不这么做，也就是在前向传播中继续跑随机二值神经元，但在反向传播中跑标准反向传播。那么在反向传播里，你用的是那些 p 和 1-p，但它们永远不需要被传到神经元外。这样训练实际上更慢，但泛化好得多。所以这是更好的做法。因此我想最后解释一下，为什么皮层神经元不发送模拟值。

cues.en: because that's always been a puzzle. And a lot of people say, well, there's no way they can do it efficiently. But actually, it takes some sugar to send a spike, because you have to send this wave of depolarization. It takes the same amount of sugar to send a spike with precise timing. That's not a good reason not to use the time. What's more, we know that there's neurons that do use very precise times. So when I localize a sound, I'm relying on the time
cues.zh: 因为这一直是个谜。很多人说，它们不可能高效地做到。但实际上，发放一个脉冲要消耗一些葡萄糖，因为你得发送这波去极化。而精确计时地发放一个脉冲，消耗的葡萄糖是一样的。这不是不用时间的好理由。更重要的是，我们知道有些神经元确实使用非常精确的时间。所以当我定位一个声音时，我依赖的是时间

cues.en: difference in time for the sound to get to my two ears. Now that's a millisecond for sound. And the difference in time to my two ears is more sort of like this. That's the difference in distance. So we're talking about a small fraction of a millisecond. And your neurons do that by sending a spike this way and a spike this way and seeing where they overlap. So they're using spike timing very precisely. So we know evolution can do that if it wants to. Also in your hippocampus, you have this.
cues.zh: 声音到达我两只耳朵的时间差。对声音来说，这是毫秒量级。而到达我两耳的时间差更接近这样。这是距离差。所以我们说的是不到一毫秒的一小部分。你的神经元做到这点，是靠从这边发放一个脉冲、从那边发放一个脉冲，然后看它们在哪里重合。所以它们非常精确地利用脉冲时序。因此我们知道，进化如果想做就能做到。还有在你的海马体里，你也有这个。

cues.en: Well, if you were a rat, which basically you are. You'd have cells that fired when you're in a particular place. And so the fact that the cell fired would tell you you were there. But when it fired relative to an oscillation tells you where you are within that place field. There's some debate about that still, but it's pretty well established. So there you're using the precise time of the spike to tell you where you are and the fact that it occurred to tell you you're
cues.zh: 嗯，如果你是一只老鼠——基本上你就是。你会有一些细胞，当你在某个特定位置时就会发放。于是细胞发放这个事实会告诉你：你在那里。但它相对于振荡何时发放，会告诉你在那个位置野里的哪里。关于这一点仍有争论，但已经相当确立。所以你在用脉冲的精确时间告诉你你在哪里，用脉冲发生这个事实告诉你你在

cues.en: somewhere around right here. So we know they can use time to spike. So I think this just isn't a plausible explanation. They can do it. There's an efficient way to do it. And they don't. Another argument is evolution just never thought of it. I mean, it just never stumbled across this idea. And I find that highly implausible. Evolution can take the same cells and turn them into teeth and eyeballs. If it can do that, using the time of a spike seems pretty obvious.
cues.zh: 就在这附近某处。所以我们知道它们能利用时间发放脉冲。所以我认为这根本不是一个合理的解释。它们能做到。有一种高效的做法。但它们没有做。另一个论点是进化从没想到过。我是说，它从没偶然碰到这个想法。而我觉得这极不可信。进化能把同样的细胞变成牙齿和眼球。如果它能做到那个，利用脉冲的时间看起来就相当显然。

cues.en: We can even think of it. So I don't believe that. My current explanation is, neurons don't send analog values because they don't want to. They're better off sending stochastic spikes. And that's because it's such a great regularizer. And what neurons are really concerned to do is fit a gazillion models to this weird data they're confronted with, average what all these models are saying, and sending stochastic spikes is a very good way to do that. OK, I'm done.
cues.zh: 我们甚至可以这样想。所以我不相信那个说法。我目前的解释是，神经元不发送模拟值是因为它们不想发。它们更倾向于发送随机脉冲。这是因为随机脉冲是非常好的正则项。神经元真正关心的，是将无数个模型拟合到所面对的这组奇怪数据上，并对所有这些模型的输出取平均，而发送随机脉冲正是实现这一点的好方法。好，我讲完了。

cues.en: So we have time for a few questions. But if you want to ask a question, you have to talk into the microphone. Oh, OK. One personal question. Another argument why cortical neurons don't send analog values is that it's more power efficient to do it stochastically. Why is it more power efficient? Because the energy is in sending this wave of depolarization down the axon. You have to sort of.
cues.zh: 我们还有时间回答几个问题。不过提问的话得对着麦克风说。哦，好的。问一个个人问题。关于大脑皮层神经元不发送模拟值的另一个论点是，采用随机方式能效更高。为什么能效更高呢？因为能量消耗在沿着轴突传递这种去极化波上。你不得不有点……

cues.en: Your sodium pump has to pump the ions back in again. No, I'm not sending the spikes like doing the work related to like aligning the spikes and like looking at various along the beam. It's not that hard. I mean, one thing that really convinced me of this is I dreamt up a little scheme so I could send I could you could time spikes carefully and you could, for example, do scalar products where it was a scalar product of a vector of synapse strengths.
cues.zh: 你的钠泵必须把离子重新泵回去。不，我说的不是发送脉冲，比如对齐脉冲或沿波束做检查这类操作。这其实并不难。我是说，真正让我确信这一点的是，我曾构思过一个小方案，可以精确控制脉冲的时间，比如做标量积，也就是突触强度向量……

cues.en: and a vector of spike times. You can do that scalar project, and then it's quite easy to convert that back into the time of a spike for the next layer. So it's not hard to dream up machinery that does it. It's just that the cortex doesn't seem to be using it. So I think there is an energy efficient way to do it. Yeah. So in the dropout case, you turn the stochasticity on during training as a regularizer, but then at test time to get the power of those models back out.
cues.zh: 和脉冲时间向量的标量积。你可以做这个标量积，然后很容易把它再转换回下一层的脉冲时间。所以构想出实现这一功能的机制并不难。只是大脑皮层似乎并没有采用它。所以我认为确实存在一种高能效的实现方式。是的。所以在 Dropout 的情况下，你在训练时开启随机性作为正则项，但在测试时为了重新发挥这些模型的能力，

cues.en: you average them, right? But if this is your conjecture for how the brain works and stochasticity is always on, it's as if it's always training. When can it cash out? How can it cash out and actually average those models to behave well at test time like right now? So to average the models, what it would need to do is run for a while and use spike rates. Basically, you need to integrate over time being stochastic. And if you look at people making decisions,
cues.zh: 你会对它们取平均，对吧？但如果这就是你对大脑运作方式的猜想，并且随机性始终开启，那它就像是一直在训练。它什么时候才能“兑现”？它怎么兑现并真正平均这些模型，从而在测试时——比如当下——表现良好？要平均这些模型，它需要做的是运行一段时间并利用脉冲频率。基本上，你需要在时间维度上对随机性进行积分。如果你观察人们做决定的过程，

cues.en: They get more accurate with time. So the way the brain, if this is why it's using stochastic spikes, the way it would have to do the model averaging is in the correct way, which is to run it several times. And so you'd get more accurate if you spent more time by averaging results over time. And psychologists have lots of evidence that you do that when you're trying to make decisions. That's why you get more accurate if you give them more time.
cues.zh: 决策准确度会随着时间推移而提高。所以如果这就是大脑使用随机脉冲的原因，那它做模型平均的方式就必须走正确的路子，也就是多运行几次。花的时间越多，通过随时间平均结果，准确度就会越高。心理学家有大量证据表明人们在做决策时确实是这样。这就是为什么给他们更多时间，准确率就会更高。

cues.en: Hi. So has the methods like this been applied to general Bolton machines, more general models like this? Well, a Bolton machine is already doing this, right? A Bolton machine is all stochastic spikes. That's true. I don't know if the spikes, the intensity of the spikes, I mean, in your case, it's 0.20% constant. But in observations, it could be very diverse, right?
cues.zh: 你好。这类方法有没有应用到通用的玻尔兹曼机，或者更通用的类似模型上？玻尔兹曼机其实已经在这么做了，对吧？玻尔兹曼机全都是随机脉冲。确实。但我不知道脉冲的强度，在你的例子中是恒定的 0.20%，但在实际观测中可能会非常多样，对吗？

cues.en: No. Spikes are pretty much all the same size. So a spike is propagated by sending a wave of depolarization down the axon. And it's a digital thing. cues.zh: 不对。脉冲的大小基本都是一样的。脉冲是通过沿轴突传递去极化波来传播的。它本质上是数字化的，即每个阶段都是数字信号。因此，只要你在这一端让它去极化、波开始向前传播，另一端输出的结果就完全是可预测的。

cues.en: what comes out the other end will stay the same, even if the action has branches and so on. So it's a sort of digital system. You put one in this end and one comes out the other end.
